source.title: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, revealing a three-stage in-context learning mechanism
source.authors: Jiajun Bao; Nicolas Boullé; To-Ni J. B. Liu; Raphael Sarfati; Christopher J. Earls

record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream PDE-prediction performance across model sizes, using a different task and metric from pretraining-loss scaling studies. It does not test the original parameter, training-token, or compute laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures PDE prediction error against context length, output length, and model size, but does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, training-token or compute scaling, or a compute-optimal allocation. The context-length results are recorded as findings outside the listed claim versions. The study also reports comparisons with numerical solvers and repeat-based baselines.
record.test_reason: The study compares three Llama-3 sizes (1B, 3B, 8B) on a new downstream task, zero-shot PDE continuation. It reports that larger models are more accurate and more robust to output length, which bears on V6 in a new setting. The comparison is qualitative, uses only three off-the-shelf checkpoints and fits no scale law. The study's 'in-context scaling laws' concern context and output length, not training scale, so they do not test V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that text-trained LLMs continue PDE dynamics zero-shot. They describe 'in-context scaling laws': accuracy improves with temporal context and degrades with spatial output length, and multi-step error grows algebraically. Entropy reveals a three-stage progression: syntax imitation, exploration, then consolidation. They add that larger Llama-3 models are more robust to output length, an effect mainly seen within one family. Their 'scaling laws' refer to context and output length, not model or training scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates zero-shot PDE forecasts and RMSE across inference context, output length, and model sizes. It does not fit pretraining-loss power laws or vary training compute, parameter counts as a training sweep, or training tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction error varies with temporal context length, spatial output length, and model size. The authors also report that errors differ slightly between similar-sized models from different families.

fits_no_version.finding: One-step RMSE falls roughly as O(1/NT) with temporal context length, and grows roughly as O(NX) with spatial output length. Multi-step rollout error grows algebraically with horizon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero-shot in-context prediction error of LLMs on serialized PDE data scales as a power of context length and output length.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean token entropy grows with output length, steepest for 1B and slowest for 8B. In multi-step rollouts, 1B keeps higher entropy than larger models (Fig 5b, Fig 24).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models give more confident token predictions on in-context numerical continuation.

record.peer_reviewed: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and Partial Differential Equations (AI&PDE)
record.problems: The evidence for model-size scaling is qualitative and mainly presented in figures, with no fitted quantitative relation to downstream performance. The main size comparison is within one model family; similar-sized models from different families show slightly different errors.

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining loss and no training sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: no fits extrapolated across training runs.
All of it: no compute-optimal allocation.
All of it: architecture shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
All of it: the models are text-pretrained and evaluated zero-shot. No power law in parameters, data or compute is fitted in another modality or training regime.

No quantitative law of downstream performance against parameters, compute or pretraining loss. Only three sizes are compared, and they are not a controlled training sweep. The relation to pretraining loss is not tested.

missing.what: Comparison with repeat baselines: 8B and 3B beat both baselines across NX, while 1B degrades and falls below temporal repeat at fine NX.
Multi-step rollouts: 1B fails to preserve spatiotemporal structure and shows systematic errors, while 3B and 8B track the dynamics.
Instruction-tuned variants: the smaller 3B and 1B Instruct models lose accuracy relative to their base models, while 8B Instruct does not.
Phi-4-14B accuracy relative to the 3B models. The text does not say the larger 14B model is more accurate.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak, incidental test of V6. There are three checkpoints, which differ in training data and recipe as well as size, and no quantitative fit. The record's T2 is wrong because the study is not aimed at the scaling question; T3 fits better. R1–R3 correctly carry no version. The record's V6 label grouping is reasonable, but the states of R4–R6 are better read jointly as an observed qualitative ordering.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or training compute.
Extrapolating pretraining-loss fits from small training runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations at fixed training compute.
Architecture effects on held-out pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes. Applying text-trained models to PDE prediction is not a test of those training-regime laws.
The study evaluates PDE forecasting, not a range of conventional downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss; it does not fit a quantitative scale-prediction law.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fit choices, and bending of those curves.

rows.note: The text reports that RMSE decreases consistently as context increases; this is an in-context effect, not a test of pretraining-loss scaling.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: One-step Allen–Cahn prediction across spatial output lengths.

conditions.value: NX varied across 20 evenly spaced values from 2 to 40

rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals over 50 random initial conditions
rows.note: The text says error growth is steepest for this model within the Llama-3 family; its accuracy drops more at finer discretizations.
rows.check: This row is one point in the size ordering, not a partial effect. The text says 1B has the steepest RMSE growth with NX, the smallest of the three Llama-3 models. Judged jointly with R5 and R6, the within-family ordering is observed qualitatively, with no numbers.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B
rows.operation_detail: One-step Allen–Cahn prediction across spatial output lengths.

conditions.value: NX varied across 20 evenly spaced values from 2 to 40

rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals over 50 random initial conditions
rows.note: The reported family-level trend is that the larger Llama-3 models are more robust to longer outputs; the text does not give a separate numerical trend for this checkpoint.
rows.check: This is the middle point of a within-family ordering the text states qualitatively. On its own the row cannot show a size effect, so R4–R6 should be read together. Partial understates the stated ordering.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: One-step Allen–Cahn prediction across spatial output lengths.

conditions.value: NX varied across 20 evenly spaced values from 2 to 40

rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals over 50 random initial conditions
rows.note: The text says this model has slower error growth than the smaller models, but does not fit a quantitative relation between downstream performance and model size.
rows.check: The text says 8B shows the slowest error growth, 'improved robustness to output length'. This is observed qualitatively. The lack of a fitted law is an untested part of V6, not a partial effect.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B
rows.operation_detail: One-step prediction across spatial output lengths in a comparison with other model families.
rows.note: The text says similar-sized Llama-3.2-3B and SmolLM-3-3B have slightly different quantitative errors, and that the size effect is chiefly apparent within a model family.
rows.check: This is a comparison of similar-sized models across families, so it cannot show a scale effect. It only shows that family matters at fixed size. No direction or number is given.

rows.subject: SmolLM-3-3B
rows.operation_detail: One-step prediction across spatial output lengths in a comparison with other model families.
rows.note: The text reports slightly different errors from the similarly sized Llama-3.2-3B model, without stating a numerical difference or direction.
rows.check: Same as R7: SmolLM-3-3B versus Llama-3.2-3B at equal size differ 'slightly', with no direction stated. The row cannot show a size effect.

relationships.condition: Llama-3 base family (1B, 3B, 8B), one-step Allen–Cahn prediction across spatial output lengths
relationships.reason: Error growth with NX is steepest for 1B and slowest for 8B, so larger models perform better (R4–R6). Figure 18 (not in the rows) shows 1B falling below a temporal-repeat baseline while 3B and 8B stay above it. This evidence is qualitative and figure-based.
relationships.display_finding: Error grew fastest with spatial output length for 1B and slowest for 8B, while 1B fell below the temporal-repeat baseline and 3B and 8B remained above it.

relationships.condition: Models from different families at similar parameter counts (Llama-3.2-3B vs SmolLM-3-3B)
relationships.reason: The authors say the size effect holds 'primarily' within a family, and similar-sized cross-family models differ. Parameter count alone does not predict performance (R7–R8).
relationships.display_finding: Similar-sized Llama-3.2-3B and SmolLM-3-3B differed in performance, with size effects holding primarily within model families.
